scenes.title: Inventory costs and the EOQ model
scenes.subtitle: How much should a business order each time?
narration: Welcome to lesson one of Unit 3, Inventory Management.
By the end of this lesson, you will know what inventory costs a business, and how the economic order quantity tells you exactly how much to order each time.

scenes.definition: The stock of materials a firm holds to meet future demand.
scenes.gloss: Everything a business keeps on its shelves so it can serve customers tomorrow.

points.text: MRO supplies: maintenance, repair and operating items

narration: Let's start with the basic idea. Your notes define inventory as the stock of materials a firm holds to meet future demand.
In simple words, it is everything a business keeps on its shelves so that it can serve customers tomorrow.
It comes in four forms: raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods.
The fourth is M R O supplies, which means maintenance, repair and operating items, like spare parts and cleaning material.

scenes.heading: The three costs of inventory

items.text: **Ordering cost (S)**: placing and receiving one order
items.sub: Paperwork, transport, inspection. Same whatever the order size.

items.text: **Holding cost (H)**: keeping one unit for one year
items.sub: Storage, insurance, obsolescence, cost of capital.

callout.title: Think of a kirana store
callout.text: Order rice every day: many trips to the wholesaler. Order a year's rice at once: the back room is full and money is stuck in sacks.

narration: Your notes list three costs. First, the ordering cost, S. It is the cost of placing and receiving one order, and it stays the same whatever the order size.
Second, the holding cost, H. That is the cost of keeping one unit in stock for one year, such as storage, insurance and the money tied up in it.
Third, the shortage cost: the sales and goodwill you lose when you cannot meet demand.
Here is an everyday picture, which is my example, not from your notes. A kirana store that orders rice every day makes many trips to the wholesaler.
But a store that buys a whole year's rice at once fills its back room and locks up its cash.

lines.text: Order a big lot this time, Ramesh. Fewer deliveries for you!
But then my godown is packed, and my money sits in sacks for months.
Then I pay for a delivery every few days. There must be a best size in between.

scenes.heading: What one order size means for stock on hand

notes.text: An order of **Q units** arrives, then demand uses it up steadily.
Big Q: fewer orders in a year, so a lower **ordering cost**.
Average stock is **Q/2**, so holding cost is **(Q/2) × H**.

narration: Let's picture this. When an order of Q units arrives, the stock jumps up, and steady demand uses it until the next order arrives.
A big Q means fewer orders a year, so the yearly ordering cost, D over Q times S, falls.
But on average you hold half the order, Q over two, so the holding cost is Q over two, times H. This graph uses the numbers from your example on page five.

scenes.heading: Two costs pulling in opposite directions

notes.text: Total cost is lowest where the two are **equal**.

narration: Now let's plot both costs against the order quantity. The blue ordering cost falls as Q grows, because you order fewer times.
The orange holding cost rises in a straight line, because you keep more stock.
Add them together and you get the total cost curve, shaped like a U.
Your notes point out that the bottom of this U is exactly where ordering cost equals holding cost. That best order size is called the economic order quantity.

scenes.heading: The EOQ formula

terms.label: Annual demand, in units per year
Holding cost per unit per year

narration: Setting ordering cost equal to holding cost and solving gives this formula. E O Q equals the square root of two D S over H.
D is the annual demand, how many units you sell in a year.
S is the cost of placing one order.
And H is the cost of holding one unit for a year. Notice H sits at the bottom, so costly storage means smaller orders.
Remember it as: square root of two times demand times ordering cost, divided by holding cost.

scenes.heading: Example 1: find the EOQ
narration: Let's solve Example 1 from page five. A distributor sells {{D}} units a year, each order costs ₹{{S}}, and holding one unit for a year costs ₹{{H}}.
Step one, write the formula.
Step two, substitute: two times {{D}} times {{S}}, divided by {{H}}.
Step three, simplify. Two times {{D}} times {{S}} is {{NUM}}, and dividing by {{H}} gives {{X}}.

narration.text: The square root of {{X}} is {{EOQ|2}}, so the distributor should order about {{EOQ|0}} units each time.

scenes.heading: Example 1: orders, timing and total cost

result.text: ordering cost = holding cost, as the theory says

narration: Now the rest of the example. Orders per year, N, is demand divided by the EOQ: {{D}} divided by {{EOQ|2}} gives {{N|2}}, so about 19 orders.
With 300 working days, that is one order every {{TBO|1}} days, roughly every 16 working days.
The yearly ordering cost is {{N|2}} orders times ₹{{S}}, which is ₹{{OC|2}}.
The holding cost is half of {{EOQ|2}}, times ₹{{H}}, which is also ₹{{HC|2}}.

narration.text: So the total annual cost is ₹{{TC|2}}. And as your notes say, at the EOQ the two costs are exactly equal.

scenes.heading: Remember

items.text: Ordering cost is per order; holding cost is per unit per year
Total cost $TC = \frac{D}{Q}S + \frac{Q}{2}H$ is lowest where the two costs are equal
Example 1: order **{{EOQ|0}} units**, about **19 times** a year, total cost **₹{{TC|2}}**

narration: Let's recap. Ordering cost is paid per order, and holding cost per unit per year.
The total cost is lowest where these two costs are equal.
That point is the E O Q, the square root of two D S over H.
In our example, the distributor orders {{EOQ|0}} units, about 19 times a year, for a total cost of ₹{{TC|2}}. In the next lesson, we'll see when to place each order.
